studio.practice.need: The job becomes a specification: the pins, what each output must be for every input, how fast, at what power, on which process. Every later step is checked against it, so a job left vague here comes back later as a bug.
studio.practice.logic: Chips are described in a hardware description language, most often Verilog or SystemVerilog. The lab's lines are Verilog with the ceremony left out; here is your description in Verilog, as Yosys, an open program that turns descriptions into gates, would read it.
studio.practice.check: Designers simulate (run the description on chosen inputs), measure coverage (how much of the design the tests reached) and, for the riskiest parts, prove properties with mathematics (formal verification). Even so, in 2024 only 14% of projects worked the first time they were made.
studio.practice.gates: Synthesis maps the description onto standard cells: ready-made gates from the PDK (process design kit), the factory's kit for designers, each cell drawn, measured and modelled by the factory. In the open flow Yosys does it, then every path is timed against the clock, and its power estimated: every wire that switches costs energy, more at a faster clock.
studio.practice.layout: Placement and routing (OpenROAD, in the open flow) put the cells in rows and draw every wire; then a design rule check measures every shape against the PDK's rules. In SKY130, metal 1 must be at least 0.14 µm wide and 0.14 µm from its neighbour. Your tile keeps those by drawing on a grid of tracks; the rules below are the ones a grid cannot promise.
studio.practice.masks: The layout is written out as one file of shapes, layer by layer, and sent: tapeout. The open path runs all the way: an open PDK (SKY130 since 2020, GF180 since 2022), open tools (Yosys for gates, OpenROAD for placement, routing and timing, OpenLane, now LibreLane, running them in order) and shared runs such as Tiny Tapeout.
studio.need.spec: {ins} inputs, {outs} outputs: {n} input patterns, each with the answer the job wants.
studio.need.seq: {ins} inputs, {outs} outputs and a clock: a test of {n} ticks, each with the answers the job wants.
studio.need.free: No specification: this job says what goes in and what comes out, but not what is right.
studio.logic.lines: {v} lines of Verilog for {n} of the lab's: the same wires, with a module around them and every pin declared.
studio.logic.core: The core's description is the program it runs; this is its arithmetic slice.
studio.check.all: All {n} input patterns tried: for a circuit this small, that is a proof.
studio.check.seq: {n} ticks of one test tried: a test can still miss a state the design can reach.
studio.check.core: {n} test programs run: right on every one of them, but a processor has more programs than anyone could try.
studio.check.cov: These patterns would catch {caught}% of the faults a factory could leave inside the gates.
studio.check.none: The description does not read yet, so nothing can be tried.
studio.k.gates: In time? The longest chain against the clock

studio.gates.chain.other: Longest chain: {n} cells, {logic} ps, from {from} to {to}.

studio.gates.fmax: The fastest clock it could take: about {fmax} MHz.
studio.gates.chained: Copied {n} times in a row, each carry feeding the next as in a 32-bit adder, it needs {need} ps: about {fmax} MHz.
studio.gates.core: The core's adder is {n} slices in a row, and the carry passes through every one of them in each tick.

fab.title: At the factory
fab.need: It will be made at a 130 nanometre factory, on a shared run with many other designs: the line in the journey is the one it will travel.
fab.logic: Every line becomes transistors the factory must print: your design needs about {transistors}.
fab.check: Passing every check makes a perfect design, not a perfect chip. The factory leaves defects: a speck, a missing via, one wire stuck. Make a copy at the factory and see what happens.
fab.checkCore: Your core passes its programs as designed. Made at the factory, one copy may have a wire stuck in one slice; then real programs go wrong.
fab.gates: How fast it runs depends on the switches the factory makes. On this process the longest path takes about {ps} picoseconds, so it could tick about {mhz} million times a second. A hotter, older or unluckier chip is slower.
fab.gatesCore: Your slice is copied 32 times: one flaw in the design, or one stuck wire from the factory, is copied into every add.
fab.layout: Your layout covers about {area} square micrometres. On the wafer, a speck that lands on a chip ruins it: the bigger the layout, the more chips a speck can ruin.
fab.masks: These {masks} masks are made once and printed onto every wafer, at the Print station. On a shared run, everyone shares their cost.
fab.defect: This copy came out with one wire stuck at {v}: {wrong} of {total} answers are now wrong, though the design is right.
fab.caught: Your {vectors} test patterns catch it: at the Test station this chip would be marked bad, not shipped. A big chip cannot be tested this completely.
fab.defectCore: This copy came out with one wire stuck in slice {bit}: only {passed} of {total} test programs still give the right answer. The design was perfect.
place.dc.campus.d: Three halls, coolers on their roofs, and a substation feeding them as much power as a town.
place.dc.hall.d: Rows of racks. Cold air rises through the floor in front of them; the hot air is closed in behind.
place.dc.rack.d: Two metres of servers: a network switch at the top, power at the bottom, liquid cooling up the back.
place.dc.server.d: One tray slides out: fans at the front, then the board, the accelerator under its heat sink.
place.dc.board.d: Lift the heat sink: the accelerator's package, power stages around it, memory beside it.
place.dc.chip.d: Under its lid: the die, copies of one compute tile, with stacks of memory right beside it.
place.phone.phone.d: About 150 mm of glass and metal, under 8 mm thick. Everything a computer needs has to fit inside, and run all day on one battery.
place.phone.inside.d: Open it like a book: the battery fills most of it. The computer is the small board at the top, beside the cameras.
place.phone.board.d: Lift the metal shields: the phone's chip with its memory on top, the power chip, the modem, the storage, and hundreds of tiny parts.
place.phone.chip.d: Lift the memory off and clear the package: one die, about 11 mm a side, with a district for each kind of work.
place.car.car.d: An electric car on its road. Under the paint, dozens of small computers each do one job, and must keep doing it for the car's whole life, in heat, cold and shaking.
place.car.inside.d: Cut away the roof and the near side: the floor is the battery, the motor sits at the back wheels, and control units everywhere are joined by the wiring. Follow the one in the driver's footwell.
place.car.unit.d: Lift the lid off its sealed metal case: a plug for the car's wires, one small chip that decides, and big parts that switch real current.
place.car.chip.d: Clear the black package: the die sits on a metal pad, joined to the legs by wires finer than a hair. Two small cores, the memory that keeps its program, and its senses.
door.look.d: The place, and its levels one inside the next
look.supply.d: Follow a chip across the world, then stop a place and see what waits.
look.plan.d: Every piece of the shared computer: who built it, and what is still open.

game.allDone: Every challenge is done. The loop goes on: the shared computer still has open jobs at the Lab.
game.lab.do: The community is building one small computer in the open, piece by piece: {built} of {total} pieces are built. Each open job is a piece anyone can design, a person or an AI. The check decides.
game.engineWanted: No engine can check this piece yet. Writing one is a job too.
game.village.do: Every house is a design in the ledger: lit while it holds a record, red once a case has broken it, with a small green light for every try it survived. A watchtower is a case that guards a piece; a lantern is a question someone asked. The loudest call glows.
game.idea.do: This sandbank is for what the island does not have yet: a new place, a new challenge, a new question. Propose it; if the community takes it up, it grows here.
game.idea.title: An idea for the island
game.noLook: Nothing to look inside here yet.
game.toastJob: Checked. Keep it, and it can join the ledger.
game.jobs: Open jobs for the shared computer
game.jobsD: a person or an AI can take one
game.grows: Finish it and the island grows: {what}
game.aiNote: An AI can be wrong. The check decides.
game.wrongRows: {bad} of {n} input patterns give a wrong answer. Look at the crossed-out outputs.
game.aiWrong: The AI sounded sure, and it was wrong. This is why every design is checked.
game.built: The engine built it from {cells} gates and {transistors} transistors. Its slowest path takes about {ps} picoseconds, {depth} gates one after another.
game.oneChip: You have one chip: its settings carry from challenge to challenge, so a change for one goal can undo another.
game.own.half: Adds two bits: 0 + 0, 0 + 1, 1 + 0 and 1 + 1, giving a sum and a carry. The first building block of every calculator and processor. This description has one bug: check it, and the table shows which row goes wrong.
game.job.goal: Design this piece of the shared computer: {job}. When the check passes, keep it as an entry of the ledger.
game.spot.d: The factory made four copies of the full adder, and one is broken. Run up to {tests} test patterns on all four, then say which copy is broken.
game.spot.fine: Copy {chip} is fine. Look for the column that differs from what it should be.
game.spot.missed: None of your patterns caught it: the broken copy gets these right. Real testers face this too: which few patterns catch the most faults?
game.spot.found: Yes: copy {chip} is broken, and your patterns caught it.
grow.masks: your first masks, on a truck from the studio's mask house to the factory
game.tape.k: From your description to the factory
game.tape.layout: placed and joined by {wire} steps of wire
game.tape.masks: about {n} masks, one for each layer
game.tape.fab: {n} laps round the line, one per mask, printed onto every wafer
game.tape.dust: At the factory, one speck of dust can leave a wire stuck at {v}. In that copy, {wrong} of {n} input patterns give a wrong answer, and it looks exactly like the others.
game.tape.spot: Find a copy like it at the test house
chipx.title: Inside a chip, layer by layer
chipx.order: {steps}: step {n} of {total}, from the silicon up (go up a level and the next step lays it on).
chipx.yours.print: Your {name}'s {gates} gates are printed here, with about {masks} masks.
chipx.yours.wires: Its gates are joined here by {wire} steps of wire.
chipx.yours.gate: Your {name} is down here: {gates} gates, built from {transistors} switches (transistors).
chipx.yoursNone: Design something at the studio, and you will find it in these layers
game.spot.yoursD: These are copies of the full adder you designed at the studio, made by the factory with your masks.
game.spot.labD: These are copies of the lab's full adder. Win the full adder at the studio, and the copies here become yours.
game.spot.why: The factory left one wire inside it stuck at {v}: every gate that wire feeds sees {v}, whatever the inputs say. The patterns that caught it are the ones that needed that wire to be the other value.
board.up: Back up to the data centre
board.reuseLabel: How many times each number is used
board.gauge.moving: Energy of one multiply-add spent fetching
board.story.intro: One board, in one rack. Almost everything on it is here to feed [[chip|one chip]]. Tap any part, or go on.
board.story.die: Under the lid, [[die|the die]] does the arithmetic: thousands of small cores, each multiplying and adding. One multiply-and-add costs about {math} picojoules, a millionth of a millionth of a joule.
board.story.hbm: The numbers live in [[hbm|these memory stacks]], a few millimetres from the die. Fetching what one sum needs costs {move} picojoules: {ratio} times the sum itself. Watch the cores: most of them wait.
board.story.reuse: Now suppose each number, once it has arrived, is used [[#reuse]] times before the next one is fetched. Before you drag it: how much more work does the chip get done?
board.story.reuse.b: That many times more, up to a point
board.story.reuse.wrong: Not quite: drag the number and watch the cores.
board.story.reuse.why: Used once, the cores are {b1}% busy; used 16 times, {b16}%. After that the arithmetic itself is the limit, but each sum still costs less energy to feed.
board.story.links: A chip this hungry is never alone: [[links|these links]] join it to the other boards, so thousands of chips can work on one problem, and wait on each other.
board.story.power: All of it runs on current from [[vrm|these power stages]], and much of that current goes into moving numbers, not adding them.

game.op.and.d: AND: 1 only when both inputs are 1
game.op.xor.d: XOR: 1 when exactly one input is 1
game.tap.half: It adds two bits, but one gate is wrong. Tap a gate to change it: the table checks all four sums after every tap.
game.tap.vote: The output should be 1 when at least two inputs are 1, but one pair is missing. Add the piece that covers it: the table checks all eight patterns after every tap.
game.tap.full: The sum should be 1 when an odd number of the three inputs are 1, but the sum line forgets one input. Add the piece that brings it in.
game.tap.pieces: Pieces to add to the first line (tap again to take one off)
game.break.goal: Find a case that makes this design answer wrong.
game.break.kicker: The ledger · a design that passed its check
game.break.why: It passed all {ticks} ticks of the lab's test, so it was let in. A test tries some cases, never all of them. Set the inputs tick by tick, and watch what it should show and what it does.
game.break.was: {who} found a case that breaks it, and that case is part of the check now. The design stays here so you can find the case too.
game.break.cols: Inputs: {ins}. Shown: {outs}, as they stand before each tick.
game.break.hint: A test checks only the moments it visits. See where the lab's test changes an input, and change one at a moment it never tried.
game.break.found: Broken at tick {n}: it should show {want} and shows {got}.
game.break.then: No test the lab ran would ever have shown this. Keep the case and it joins the check: every design after this one has to pass it.
game.break.too: You found it too. {who} added this case to the check.
game.break.holds: Right on all {n} ticks so far.
game.toastBreak: You broke it. Keep the case, and the check grows.
game.break.heldNote: A try that fails is worth keeping too: it says what this design has survived, and where the next person need not look.

room.title: Inside the studio
room.outside.d: The studio's ground floor, opened: a corner for each step of a design, in order along the room, from the job at the west end to the mask house beside the road to the factory.
room.need.d: The job: a wall of notes and a table to talk round. Before anything is drawn, someone writes down what the chip must do, and for whom.
room.logic.d: Describe: desks where the circuit is written as text in a hardware language. The free desk at the front is yours.
room.check.d: Check: machines run every pattern of inputs through the description, and the wall shows the answers as waves, right or wrong.
room.gates.d: Gates: a program turns the description into small ready-made circuits, and people read its drawing for what it got wrong.
room.layout.d: Layout: a table that is a screen, where the cells are placed and wired as they will lie on the silicon.
room.masks.d: The masks: a plate of glass for each layer, its pattern in chrome. From this bay they go by road to the factory.

fab.ui.lead: Software changes the same day. Everything else has to be made first, and where it is made sets how many tries fit in a year.
fab.ui.none: Nothing in this machine needs making: its parts are software or bought ready-made. A try takes a day.
fab.ui.grown: Living matter is grown from cells, not made in a fab: how long a try takes is not known here.
fab.ui.guessDays: {low} days a try, if the guess holds
fab.ui.setup: a line costs {x} of a giant fab to set up
fab.ui.note: Energy here is counted as if every part were made at 45 nm. Lines this coarse cost more energy per step: try here, then make the one that wins at a giant fab.
fab.name.giant.d: The fabs that make today's chips: every form, at the finest lines, and months for each try.
fab.name.small.d: Minimal Fab: a line of small tools on half-inch wafers, with no cleanroom.
fab.name.flexible.d: Thin-film circuits printed on plastic: slower and larger than silicon, made in days.
fab.name.desk.d: Chips made at home, or by machines a factory of fabs turns out: a try a day, perhaps.
fab.claim.giantDays: 18 to 26 weeks from a finished design to tested wafers.
fab.claim.giantCost: The yardstick: what every other line is set against.
fab.claim.smallReal: In use: no cleanroom, half-inch wafers, sold for prototyping.
fab.claim.smallCost: A hundredth to a thousandth of the cost of a giant fab, its makers say.
fab.claim.smallDays: A few days to two weeks a try: a guess; we found no source.
fab.claim.flexDays: Under 48 hours a run; under a week to tested wafers.
fab.claim.flexWeek: The same source sets silicon at 18 to 26 weeks.
fab.claim.flexCost: A hundredth of the cost of a standard fab, its maker says.
fab.claim.deskReal: One person made a chip of 1,200 transistors in a garage, at 10 µm.
fab.claim.deskFab2: A company is building a factory that makes small fabs and the tools in them.
fab.claim.deskDays: A day to a week a try: a guess.
fab.claim.deskCost: A ten-thousandth of a giant fab: a guess.

whatif.lever.demand.d: How much AI computing the world wants to buy
whatif.lever.hbm.d: The stacked memory every big AI chip needs
whatif.lever.elec.d: What data centers pay for power
whatif.lever.node.d: The leading foundry's next process arrives late
whatif.lever.mature.d: Ordinary chips on older processes: car, appliance and power chips
whatif.ind.perfw: Performance per watt of the newest chips
whatif.ind.archgain: Gains that must come from design, not the node
whatif.ind.designcost: Cost to design a leading chip
whatif.ind.newarch: Push for new ways to compute
whatif.why.aidemand.memtight: Almost all HBM goes into AI chips, so more AI demand means more HBM wanted.
whatif.why.hbm.memtight: Less HBM made with the same demand leaves a bigger gap.
whatif.why.delay.memtight: When the next node is late, designers add chiplets and bigger packages instead, which need more CoWoS packaging and HBM.
whatif.why.memtight.memprice: Memory makers move wafers to HBM, which takes about three times the wafer area of ordinary DRAM per bit, so all memory gets scarce. In late 2025 and early 2026 DRAM contract prices rose by about half each quarter.
whatif.why.memprice.memprofit: When prices rise and costs do not, profits rise faster than prices. SK hynix reported a 76% operating margin in mid-2026.
whatif.rule.memprice.devprice: memory is part of every device
whatif.why.memprice.devprice: Memory is a slice of what a phone or PC costs to build. In 2026 analysts expected PC prices to rise about 6–8% after DRAM prices more than doubled.
whatif.why.mature.devprice: A product missing one cheap chip cannot ship, so the few that do ship cost more.
whatif.rule.mature.cars: one missing chip stops a car
whatif.why.mature.cars: A car needs hundreds of chips, most on mature processes. In 2021 the shortage cost carmakers about 7.7 million vehicles.
whatif.why.aidemand.aiship: Chipmakers build to what customers order.
whatif.why.hbm.aiship: Each AI chip needs its HBM stacks. Shipments follow whichever is scarcer: orders or memory.
whatif.why.memtight.gpuprice: When buyers want more chips than can be built, prices rise.
whatif.rule.memprice.gpuprice: HBM is a big part of the bill
whatif.why.memprice.gpuprice: HBM is one of the largest costs in making an AI chip.
whatif.why.delay.perfw: A new node gives about 25–30% lower power at the same speed and comes every two to three years, so each year of delay forgoes roughly 12%.
whatif.why.perfw.energytoken: Chips that do less per watt use more energy for each answer.
whatif.rule.perfw.archgain: design must make up the gap
whatif.why.perfw.archgain: If the node gives less, the gain has to come from architecture: chiplets, specialized units, smarter dataflow.
whatif.why.aiship.aicompute: Computing power added grows with the chips installed.
whatif.why.perfw.aicompute: Data centers are limited by power, so less efficient chips do less work in the same power.
whatif.why.aiship.dcpower: More AI chips running means more electricity used.
whatif.why.dcpower.grid: Data centers already draw a growing share of electricity; more demand strains grids and new connections.
whatif.rule.elec.costtoken: power is about 7% of the cost
whatif.why.elec.costtoken: In an AI data center, electricity is only about 7% of the yearly cost; the chips and servers are about 60%.
whatif.why.energytoken.costtoken: More energy per answer, at the same electricity price.
whatif.rule.gpuprice.costtoken: chips are about 60% of the cost
whatif.why.gpuprice.costtoken: Chips and servers are about 60% of what an AI data center costs each year, so their price matters most.
whatif.why.gpuprice.custom: Expensive GPUs push big buyers to design their own chips, like Google's TPU, AWS Trainium and Microsoft Maia.
whatif.why.delay.designcost: Chips planned for the new node must be moved to an older one or wait, and both cost engineering time.
whatif.why.delay.rivals: When Intel's 10 nm slipped from 2016 to 2019, AMD (making chips at TSMC) and Apple (with its own chips) moved ahead.
whatif.why.mature.fabinvest: After the 2021 shortage, chipmakers built a wave of new capacity for mature chips.
whatif.why.aidemand.fabinvest: AI demand pays for new leading-edge fabs.
whatif.why.memprice.fabinvest: High memory prices pay for new memory fabs.
whatif.why.fabinvest.tools: Lithography and other tools are ordered years before a fab starts.
whatif.why.fabinvest.engineers: Each new fab needs hundreds of engineers and technicians.
whatif.why.energytoken.newarch: When each answer costs more energy, designs that save energy are worth more.
whatif.why.memtight.newarch: Scarce memory rewards designs that need less of it.
whatif.why.memtight.spatial: Chips like Cerebras' wafer and Groq's LPU keep the model in on-chip SRAM and need no HBM.
whatif.why.newarch.spatial: Dataflow chips move less data, which saves energy.
whatif.why.newarch.cim: Computing inside memory avoids the energy of moving data.
whatif.why.newarch.photonic: Light carries data with less energy than copper.
whatif.why.dcpower.photonic: Co-packaged optics cut the power of data-center networks.
whatif.why.newarch.neuro: Spiking chips use energy only when something happens.
whatif.why.newarch.pbits: Probabilistic chips could sample and optimize with far less energy.
whatif.why.newarch.reversible: Reversible logic is the long-term route to recycling switching energy.
whatif.preset.squeeze.d: AI demand surges and memory makers cannot keep up.
whatif.preset.cars.d: Ordinary chips run short after demand swings in the pandemic.
whatif.preset.intel.d: The next node arrives three years late, as Intel's 10 nm did.
whatif.preset.power.d: Electricity prices double where data centers are built.
whatif.puzzle.phones.t: Make phones and PCs more expensive by moving only AI demand.
whatif.puzzle.phones.done: AI demand reaches your phone through memory: makers move wafers to HBM, all DRAM gets scarce, and every device with memory costs more.
whatif.puzzle.power.t: Double the electricity price. Does the cost of an AI answer double?
whatif.puzzle.power.done: Not even close: about 7%. Power is a small part of an AI data center's cost; the chips are most of it. Power limits AI more by being unavailable than by being expensive.
whatif.puzzle.answer.t: Make each AI answer cost at least 10% more without touching the electricity price.
whatif.puzzle.answer.done: Chip prices dominate the cost of AI. Scarce memory or packaging raises them fastest.
whatif.puzzle.split.t: Find a lever that stops car factories but barely touches AI computing.
whatif.puzzle.split.done: Cars, appliances and power supplies run on mature chips made in different fabs from AI chips. The chip world is many markets, not one.
whatif.ui.title: Move one lever, and watch the change cross the sea
whatif.ui.lead: Five levers, each on the island where it is decided. Every island the change reaches rises: warm where something goes up, cool where it goes down.
whatif.ui.start: Everything is as today. Move a lever, or try one of the scenarios above.
whatif.ui.tapTag: Tap a tag over an island, or one below, to see why it changes.
whatif.ui.note: A small model of how a change spreads, not a forecast: the directions follow what happened from 2021 to 2026; the sizes are round numbers chosen to sit sensibly beside one another.
